## 1. Purpose

This procedure describes field measurement and documentation of
environmental noise levels using handheld sound level meters and
logging dosimeters. Environmental noise is an increasingly recognized
pollutant affecting human health (cardiovascular risk, sleep
disturbance, cognitive impairment) and wildlife behavior (altered
communication, habitat avoidance) [@who2018; @barber2010].

Noise monitoring in the EA Program supports community environmental
assessments, transportation corridor studies, urban ecology research,
and environmental justice analyses where noise disproportionately
affects disadvantaged communities.


## 2. Scope

- **Applies to:** Outdoor environmental noise measurements
  (community noise, traffic noise, construction noise, natural
  soundscapes) using Type 1 or Type 2 integrating sound level meters
  and personal noise dosimeters
- **Does not apply to:** Occupational noise exposure assessment
  (governed by OSHA standards and conducted by campus EH&S); indoor
  building acoustics; underwater acoustics
- **Location:** All EA Program field sites


## 3. Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                              |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------|
| PI / Field Lead   | Approve monitoring design, coordinate site access |
| Trained Personnel | Calibrate instruments, collect and document measurements |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent monitoring |


## 4. Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Traffic:** Noise monitoring often occurs near roadways. Wear a
  high-visibility vest. Never stand in a travel lane.
- **Hearing:** If monitoring near very loud sources (e.g., active
  construction, aircraft operations above 85 dBA), wear hearing
  protection.
- **Personal safety:** Monitoring in urban areas may involve working
  alone or in unfamiliar neighborhoods. Work in pairs when possible
  and inform someone of your schedule and locations.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] High-visibility vest (near roadways)
- [ ] Hearing protection (if sustained levels exceed 85 dBA)
- [ ] Closed-toed shoes
- [ ] Sun protection


## 5. Equipment and Materials

| Item                                  | Notes                          |
|:--------------------------------------|:-------------------------------|
| Integrating sound level meter (Type 1 or Type 2, IEC 61672) | With A-weighting and slow/fast time weighting |
| Acoustic calibrator (94 dB or 114 dB reference) | Matched to the microphone; calibrate before and after each session |
| Windscreen (foam cover for microphone) | Required for all outdoor measurements |
| Tripod with microphone mount          | Position microphone at 1.2--1.5 m above ground |
| Noise dosimeter (optional)            | For unattended time-integrated measurements |
| GPS unit or smartphone                | For recording coordinates      |
| Field notebook and noise monitoring data sheet | Record metadata and observations |
| Stopwatch or timer                    | For timed measurement intervals |
| Camera                                | For photo-documenting site and source conditions |
| Spare batteries                       | For the meter and calibrator   |


## 6. Procedure

### 6.1 Pre-Field Calibration

1. In a quiet indoor location, attach the acoustic calibrator to the
   microphone and turn on the calibrator
2. Adjust the sound level meter reading to match the calibrator
   reference level (e.g., 94.0 dB) per the meter's calibration
   procedure
3. Record the calibration date, time, calibrator serial number, and
   meter reading in the field notebook
4. If the meter reading deviates from the reference by more than
   0.5 dB, recalibrate or service the instrument

### 6.2 Site Setup

1. Select a measurement location that represents the receptor of
   interest (e.g., residential facade, park boundary, school
   playground)
2. Position the microphone on a tripod at 1.2--1.5 m above the ground,
   at least 3.5 m from any large reflecting surface (building wall,
   barrier, parked vehicle) to minimize reflections [@iso1996]
3. Orient the microphone toward the dominant noise source (or upward
   if the sound field is diffuse)
4. Attach the windscreen
5. Record: site ID, GPS coordinates, date, time, weather conditions
   (wind speed and direction, temperature), distance and bearing to
   the dominant source(s), ground cover, and any shielding

::: {.callout-important}
Do not measure when wind speed exceeds 5 m/s (approximately 11 mph).
Wind noise inflates readings even with a windscreen. Record the wind
speed at the start and end of each measurement period.
:::

### 6.3 Measurement Protocol

The following protocol collects standard community noise metrics.
Adjust the duration and intervals to match the study design.

1. Set the meter to: A-weighting, fast time constant, and L~eq~
   (equivalent continuous level) integration mode
2. Start the measurement and let it run for the designated period:
   - **Short-term survey:** 15 minutes per measurement location (the
     minimum recommended by most community noise standards)
   - **1-hour L~eq~:** Run for 60 minutes if comparing to local
     noise ordinance limits
   - **Long-term (24-hour):** Use a dosimeter or logging meter; deploy
     and secure the instrument
3. During the measurement, note all significant noise events in the
   field notebook: vehicle pass-bys, aircraft overflights, dog
   barking, construction activity, etc. Record the time and estimated
   duration of each event.
4. At the end of the measurement period, record the following metrics
   from the meter display:
   - L~eq~ (equivalent continuous level)
   - L~max~ (maximum level)
   - L~min~ (minimum level)
   - L~10~, L~50~, L~90~ (statistical levels, if the meter computes
     them)
5. If the meter logs time-history data, download the file after the
   session

### 6.4 Post-Field Calibration Check

1. After the final measurement at the last site, re-check the
   calibration with the acoustic calibrator
2. Record the post-measurement calibration reading. If it differs
   from the pre-measurement value by more than 1.0 dB, flag all data
   from that session for review.

### 6.5 Data Recording

For each measurement, record on the data sheet:

- Site ID, GPS coordinates, date, start/end times
- Meter make, model, serial number
- Calibration readings (pre and post)
- Weather: wind speed/direction, temperature, sky conditions
- Source description and distance
- Measurement duration and metrics (L~eq~, L~max~, L~min~, L~10~,
  L~50~, L~90~)
- Notable noise events and their times
- Observer name


## 7. Data Interpretation

| Metric  | Meaning                                           |
|:--------|:--------------------------------------------------|
| L~eq~   | Energy-averaged sound level over the measurement period; the single most important descriptor of community noise exposure |
| L~max~  | Highest instantaneous level recorded              |
| L~min~  | Lowest instantaneous level recorded               |
| L~10~   | Level exceeded 10% of the time (approximates "loud" events) |
| L~50~   | Median level                                      |
| L~90~   | Level exceeded 90% of the time (approximates background or residual noise) |
| L~dn~   | Day-night average; L~eq~ with a 10 dB penalty applied to nighttime (10 PM--7 AM) hours |

::: {.callout-note}
Community noise standards in California (Title 24, local general plans)
typically set limits in terms of L~dn~ (CNEL) or L~eq~ for specific
land use categories. A residential exterior standard of 60--65 dB
L~dn~ is common.
:::


## 8. Quality Control

- Calibrate before and after every measurement session; flag data if
  drift exceeds 1.0 dB
- Use the windscreen for all outdoor measurements
- Do not measure when wind speed exceeds 5 m/s
- Record all extraneous noise events so they can be identified in
  the time-history data
- For long-term deployments, perform a calibration check at each data
  retrieval visit
- Maintain a calibration and maintenance log for each meter


## 9. Waste Disposal

No waste is generated by noise monitoring. Dispose of used batteries
per campus battery recycling procedures.

## 12. Training Record

Before performing noise monitoring independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP and [SOP-F001](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd) in full
2. Demonstrate proper calibration of the sound level meter
3. Perform a supervised 15-minute measurement at one site, including
   correct microphone positioning, windscreen use, event logging, and
   post-calibration check
4. Demonstrate ability to read and record L~eq~, L~max~, L~min~, and
   statistical levels from the meter
5. Be signed off by the PI or field lead
